name: Apollo 11 Laser Mirror
summary: A panel of about 100 mirrors left by the first moonwalkers. Scientists on Earth still fire lasers at it to measure the distance to the Moon.
discoveries: Laser pulses bounced off the array let scientists measure the Earth–Moon distance very precisely.
Lunar laser ranging is still performed routinely to track the Moon’s orbit and rotation.

stories.kids: I’m a panel of about 100 little mirrors, left behind by the first people to walk on the Moon. I’m a passive reflector: when scientists on Earth aim a laser at me, I bounce it straight back. I’m still working!
stories.explorer: Armstrong and Aldrin placed this laser ranging reflector on July 21, 1969, near the end of their last moonwalk. It is passive: it simply returns light to where it came from. More than fifty years later, observatories still time laser pulses to measure the Moon’s distance and motion.
stories.scientist: The Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Retroreflector array (about 100 mirrors) was deployed on July 21, 1969. Timing laser pulses reflected from it gives the Earth–Moon distance; the data support studies of the Moon’s orbit and rotation and tests of general relativity.

timeline.title: Eagle lands
timeline.text: Apollo 11 touches down at Tranquility Base on July 20, 1969.

timeline.title: A mirror panel is set up
timeline.text: Armstrong and Aldrin place the laser ranging reflector, about 100 mirrors, near the end of their moonwalk.

timeline.title: Still working, 50 years later
timeline.text: Observatories on Earth still time laser pulses bounced off this panel to measure the Moon’s distance and motion.

learn.title: Who I am
learn.text: I’m a panel of about 100 little mirrors. The first moonwalkers, Armstrong and Aldrin, set me up on July 21, 1969.

learn.title: What I do
learn.text: I’m a passive reflector: when scientists aim a laser at me, I bounce the light straight back to where it came from.

learn.title: Why it matters
learn.text: By timing how long the light takes to come back, scientists measure the distance to the Moon very precisely. They still do it today, more than fifty years later!
